title: Insolvency and Business Rescue for the Cleaning Sector (UK commercial cleaning contractors, facilities/contract cleaning, janitorial, industrial and specialist cleaning firms)
research_questions: What are the specific structural and financial drivers of insolvency for UK commercial cleaning contractors 2023-2026 — labour-intensive low-margin contracts, National Living Wage rises squeezing already thin margins, TUPE liabilities on contract transfers, long client payment terms creating a wage-to-receipt cashflow gap, reliance on a small number of large contracts, and competitive tendering driving prices down? Cite sources and dates.

Name specific UK commercial cleaning or contract-cleaning companies that entered administration, CVL or other insolvency between 2023 and 2026 — company name, month/year, procedure, and stated cause. Include facilities-management and janitorial contractors. Verify from London Gazette, insolvency notices, or trade press (e.g. Cleaning Matters, Tomorrow's Cleaning, FM press).

How do UK cleaning contractors appear in the Insolvency Service company insolvency statistics for England and Wales by SIC section? Confirm they sit in SIC section N (administrative and support service activities), division 81 services to buildings and landscape, class 81.2 cleaning activities. Note section N also contains recruitment/employment agencies, the Insolvency Service reports at section level for E&W and does not isolate a cleaning sub-total; figures are England and Wales only.

What are the earliest reliable warning signs that a UK cleaning contractor is heading toward insolvency — margin erosion after wage rises not passed through in contract prices, over-reliance on one or two anchor contracts, HMRC (PAYE/NIC/VAT) arrears from the wage-cashflow gap, late client payment stretching beyond payroll dates, and TUPE-inherited liabilities on new contracts? Frame as indicators, not proof.

What insolvency and rescue options apply to UK cleaning contractors specifically, and what sector complexities arise — TUPE transfer of employees on contract loss or business sale, treatment of the workforce and employment liabilities in a CVL or administration, novation of cleaning contracts, and when a CVA (to keep contracts running) or a pre-pack sale of the contract book is realistic? Moderate all legal claims for a YMYL audience.

title: Insolvency and Business Rescue for the Haulage Sector (UK road haulage, freight transport, logistics, HGV operators, courier/distribution firms)
research_questions: What are the specific structural and financial drivers of insolvency in UK road haulage and freight 2023-2026 — fuel price volatility, thin per-mile margins, driver shortage and wage inflation, vehicle finance/HP and fleet replacement cost, tightening customer payment terms, fixed operating-licence and compliance costs, and post-Brexit/customs friction on international work? Cite sources and dates.

Name specific UK road haulage, logistics or freight companies that entered administration, CVL or other insolvency between 2023 and 2026 — company name, month/year, procedure, and stated cause. Include notable HGV operator and distribution failures. Verify from London Gazette, insolvency notices, or trade press (Motor Transport, Commercial Motor, Logistics Manager).

How do UK haulage and freight businesses appear in the Insolvency Service company insolvency statistics for England and Wales by SIC section? Confirm they sit in SIC section H (transport and storage), division 49 land transport (49.41 freight transport by road) and 52 warehousing/support. Note section H also contains taxi/passenger transport, the Insolvency Service reports at section level for E&W and does not isolate a haulage sub-total; figures are England and Wales only.

What are the earliest reliable warning signs that a UK haulage operator is heading toward insolvency — margins that do not cover fuel and finance, missed vehicle-finance or fuel-card payments, HMRC (VAT/PAYE) arrears, loss of a major contract customer, and Traffic Commissioner/operator-licence financial-standing pressure? Frame as indicators, not proof.

What insolvency and rescue options apply to UK haulage companies specifically, and what sector complexities arise — treatment of vehicle finance/HP and asset (tractor unit/trailer) repossession in a CVL or administration, operator licence and Traffic Commissioner financial-standing requirements, retention-of-title on fuel/parts, driver employment liabilities, and when restructuring vs an asset-sale closure is realistic? Moderate all legal claims for a YMYL audience.
